newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish deficit financing non-inflationary - finmin.
newsitem.headline: Polish deficit financing non-inflationary - finmin.

text.p: Poland's 1997 budget deficit, planned at 2.8 percent of gross domestic product, will be financed in a non-inflationary way, Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko said on Thursday.

"Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz's government does not propose to increase the budget deficit and its financing will be made in a non-inflationary way," Kolodko assured parliament during a debate on the 1997 tax bills.
On Wednesday, Kolodko said the government wanted to keep the 1997 budget deficit at this year's level of about 2.8 percent of GDP, rather than cut it to 2.6 percent as planned earlier.

Abandoning plans to lower the deficit was meant to help enable the government to cut next year's personal income tax levels to 20, 31 and 43 percent, depending on income, from the current 21, 33 and 45 percent.
The lower house of parliament is scheduled to vote on the tax bills later on Thursday or on Friday.

The legislation package also provides for lowering the corporate tax rate to 38 percent next year from 40 percent, scrapping a three-percent imports tax and extending the suspension of tax on income from securities until 2000.
During the tax dabate, most parliamentary caucuses backed lower taxes and even proposed slashing the lowest personal income tax level to 17 percent.
Kolodko confirmed the government had not abandoned its plan to reduce year-on-year inflation to 13 percent in December 1997 from 19.5 percent in September.
But central bank president Hanna Gronkiewicz Waltz told public television on Wednesday the higher budget deficit would jeopardise the already very ambitious 13-percent inflation goal next year.
The government plans to submit its budget draft to parliament next week. The bill's first reading is scheduled for November 14, parliament's speaker Jozef Zych said on Thursday.
